title: Erdős #1 OQ-04: Extremal Sets for Distinct Subset Sums
description: Investigates extremal sets achieving minimum N for n-element sets with distinct subset sums. Proves: factorial sequence fails (ρ → 1), vanishing average forces ρ < ε at density-1 indices, polynomial growth at low-density indices. Relates to OEIS A005318 and Conway-Guy conjecture. 15 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős #1: if A ⊆ {1,...,N} has all 2^n subset sums distinct, is N ≥ c·2^n? The minimum N values form OEIS A005318: 0,1,2,4,7,13,24,... The Conway-Guy conjecture (1968) identifies the specific extremal sets.
overview.problemStatement: Characterize extremal sets for distinct subset sums: which sequences fail to achieve the minimum N? What structure do Haight-type sets have?
overview.proofStrategy: Three results: (1) Factorial: φ(n_k)/n_k → 1, so Σ φ/n → ∞ (NOT Haight-type). (2) haight_density_one_low: if average vanishes, ρ < ε holds on a density-1 index set. (3) haight_polynomial_growth: at low-density indices, n_k grows at most polynomially.
keyInsights: **Factorial failure**: the factorial sequence n_k = (k+1)! has φ((k+1)!)/((k+1)!) → 1, so the density ratio doesn't vanish — it's NOT a Haight-type sequence.
**OEIS A005318**: the minimum values f(n) = minimum max element for n-element distinct-subset-sum sets grow like 2^n/n — the Conway-Guy conjecture identifies the argmins.
**Growth constraint**: Haight-type sequences must have certain divisibility structure at low-density indices to achieve vanishing φ-averages.

conclusion.summary: 15 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms. Structural characterization of extremal distinct-subset-sum sets proved.
conclusion.implications: Understanding extremal sets for distinct subset sums is key to resolving whether the Conway-Guy conjecture gives the true minimum.
openQuestions: Can the Conway-Guy extremal sets be verified for n ≥ 7?
Can the Erdős c·2^n conjecture for distinct subset sums be proved or disproved?
Can OEIS A005318 be computed formally for all n up to some bound?
